prompt: What is wrong with picturing a source as a shelf where finished data waits to be collected?
hint: Ask what the system was built to do.

choices.text: Shelves are for files, and most sources are databases
choices.why: The kind of source is not the problem; every kind belongs to a busy system.

choices.text: It belongs to a system busy with another job, whose owners change it
choices.why: Right: you read it as a guest, and it changes when its owners decide.

choices.text: The data on a shelf is already cleaned, which a source never is
choices.why: Cleanliness is a later question; the picture fails on ownership first.

choices.text: A shelf holds one copy, while a source keeps a backup of everything
choices.why: Backups have nothing to do with it; the source is doing another job.

prompt: Which of these sources sends its data rather than waiting to be asked?
hint: Who decides when the data moves?

choices.text: The payments provider’s API, which answers each page you request
choices.why: An API answers when asked: that is pull.

choices.text: The contractor’s nightly CSV in a directory
choices.why: The file waits in its directory until Davi’s side reads it.

choices.text: The dock sensors, which report every minute on their own
choices.why: Right: the docks decide when to speak, and Roda Livre has to be listening.

choices.text: A read replica of the app’s database
choices.why: A replica is queried, so it is pulled from.

prompt: Why is a failed push harder to notice than a failed pull?
hint: In a pull, whose request fails?

choices.text: Push sources send data in binary formats that hide errors
choices.why: The format is not the reason; the absence of a request is.

choices.text: Push failures are logged on the sender, which the data team cannot read
choices.why: Even with the sender’s log, the receiving side sees nothing happen.

choices.text: Push sources retry forever, so a failure never ends
choices.why: Retries are not the issue; silence on the receiving side is.

choices.text: No request of yours failed, so nothing on your side errors
choices.why: Right: the data just never comes, and only knowing what should have come shows it.

prompt: Match each kind of source to how Davi reads it.
hint: The table’s fourth column.

pairs.right: a query, a copy or its change log
waiting for it in a directory or a bucket

prompt: Why does the data team at Roda Livre never run analytical queries on the primary database?
hint: Who else is using that machine?

choices.text: The primary does not allow SELECT statements from other teams
choices.why: It accepts them; that is exactly the danger.

choices.text: Reading every row takes disk, memory and processor the app needs
choices.why: Right: the scan takes disk, memory and processor the app was using.

choices.text: The primary holds only today’s rides, so history is elsewhere
choices.why: It holds the current state of everything; speed is the reason, not scope.

choices.text: Analytical queries change rows by accident
choices.why: A read changes nothing, and still hurts the app.

prompt: After the second incremental copy, how many rides did `copy.db` hold?
hint: The last line of the capture.

prompt: Why did the incremental copy keep ride `R000104` after the app deleted it?
hint: What does the copy ask the source for?

choices.text: The copy ran before the delete was committed
choices.why: The second copy ran after `later.py` had committed everything.

choices.text: `INSERT OR REPLACE` refuses to remove rows it has written
choices.why: It replaces rows it is given; nobody gave it the deleted one.

choices.text: A deleted row has no newer `updated_at` to find
choices.why: Right: it is simply not there to be selected.

choices.text: The watermark was set to the wrong time zone
choices.why: The watermark worked: it found both changed rows.

prompt: A new screen in the app lets staff move a ride to another station, but the code forgets to update `updated_at`. What does the incremental copy do?
hint: The copy trusts one column.

choices.text: Raises an error the next time it compares the two databases
choices.why: The copy prints counts; it does not compare contents, and the counts still agree.

choices.text: Keeps the old station, and says nothing about it
choices.why: Right: a change with no newer `updated_at` is invisible to it.

choices.text: Copies the ride twice, once per station
choices.why: It never sees the change, so it copies nothing new.

choices.text: Picks up the change on the next run, because the row is newer
choices.why: The row is only newer if `updated_at` says so, and here it does not.

prompt: Which of these would let the data team’s copy find out that ride `R000104` was cancelled? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three were named in the section.

choices.text: The app marks cancelled rides with `deleted_at` instead of deleting them
choices.why: Yes: a soft delete is an update the copy sees.

choices.text: A weekly full copy, compared with the incremental one
choices.why: Yes: the full copy holds what the source holds.

choices.text: Reading the database’s log of changes
choices.why: Yes: a delete is a change, and the log has it.

choices.text: Running the incremental copy every five minutes instead of every hour
choices.why: More often is still blind: the deleted row is never there to select.

prompt: A database built to serve an application’s many small, fast reads and writes is called an ___ database.
hint: Online transaction processing.

prompt: What does a change data capture reader read?
hint: Not the table.

choices.text: The tables, every few seconds, looking for new rows
choices.why: That is a fast incremental copy, with the same blind spot.

choices.text: The log the database writes of every change
choices.why: Right: the record of every change, deletes included.

choices.text: The app’s source code, to see which queries it runs
choices.why: CDC reads what the database recorded, not the app’s code.

choices.text: A nightly backup of the whole database
choices.why: A backup is a full copy of state, not a stream of changes.

prompt: Why does trigger-based CDC cost the app more than reading the database’s log?
hint: Where does a trigger run?

choices.text: Triggers only work on tables with fewer than a million rows
choices.why: There is no such limit; the cost is per change, not per table size.

choices.text: Triggers send every change over the network to the data team
choices.why: The trigger writes to a table in the same database; the reader comes later.

choices.text: Each trigger adds a write of its own inside the app’s transaction, on every ride
choices.why: Right: the log is written anyway, the trigger’s row is not.

choices.text: Triggers lock the table until the data team has read the change
choices.why: They do not wait for any reader.

prompt: A CDC reader on Roda Livre’s PostgreSQL stops on Friday night and nobody notices until Monday. What is the risk to the app?
hint: The database keeps something until the reader takes it.

choices.text: The app’s tables are locked until the reader returns
choices.why: Writes go on; it is what they leave behind that piles up.

choices.text: The weekend’s rides are lost from the database
choices.why: The rides are safe in the tables; the log is what grows.

choices.text: The log piles up on the primary’s disk until it fills
choices.why: Right: the database keeps the log until the reader comes back.

choices.text: The replicas stop receiving changes along with the reader
choices.why: Replicas follow the log on their own; they are not waiting for the CDC reader.

prompt: A CDC pipeline is switched on today. How does it get the rides that already existed last year?
hint: What does the log hold?

choices.text: It reads the log back to the day the database was created
choices.why: The log holds recent changes, not the history of every row.

choices.text: It starts from one full copy, then follows the log
choices.why: Right, and follows the log from the moment that copy was taken.

choices.text: It asks the app to update every old row so they appear as changes
choices.why: That would touch every row of the app’s tables for the data team’s sake.

choices.text: It does not need them, because CDC is for new data
choices.why: A copy without the old rows answers no question about last year.

prompt: Put in order what happens to the cancellation of ride `R000104`, from the app to the data team.
hint: The log is written before the table changes.
items: the database writes the change to its log
the row leaves the rides table
the CDC reader takes the log entry
trap: The reader comes last, and it still sees the delete, because the log keeps it after the row is gone.

prompt: What does an answer with status `429` ask the client to do?
hint: Too Many Requests.

choices.text: Wait before asking again
choices.why: Right: often for the seconds `Retry-After` names.

choices.text: Send a new token
choices.why: A wrong token is `401`.

choices.text: Skip that page
choices.why: Skipping would lose its rows without a word.

choices.text: Ask for a bigger page
choices.why: A bigger page is a heavier request, not a slower one.

prompt: In `walk.py`, why does the `continue` after a `429` leave `page` unchanged?
hint: Which page was refused?

choices.text: So the server can reset its request counter
choices.why: The server counts on its own; the client is not managing it.

choices.text: Because `page` is read-only inside a `try` block
choices.why: Variables are not read-only in a `try`; this is a choice.

choices.text: So the page the server refused is asked for again rather than skipped
choices.why: Right: moving on would skip its rides and report six.

choices.text: To avoid asking for a page past the last one
choices.why: `next` being empty is what stops the loop at the end.

prompt: Where does `walk.py` take its API token from, and why?
hint: Code is copied and committed.

choices.text: A constant at the top of the file, so it is easy to change
choices.why: A token in code travels with every copy and commit of it.

choices.text: The environment, so that it stays out of the code itself
choices.why: Right: in production, a secret store does the same job.

choices.text: A file in the git repository, beside the program
choices.why: In the repository is exactly where a token is readable by anyone who has it.

choices.text: The server sends it on the first request
choices.why: The client proves who it is; the server does not hand out its own key.

prompt: How many requests did `walk.py` send to collect the three pages?
hint: Count the lines that start with `page`.

prompt: An API lists charges newest first, numbered by page. While a client walks the pages, two new charges are made. What happens to the client’s copy?
hint: Every older charge moves two places down the list.

choices.text: Two charges appear twice
choices.why: Right: the end of one page slides onto the start of the next. A cursor would not.

choices.text: The API refuses the walk with an error until it is restarted
choices.why: Nothing errors; the pages just shift.

choices.text: The two new charges are added at the end of the last page
choices.why: Newest first puts them on page 1, which the client has already read.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because page numbers are fixed when the walk begins
choices.why: A page number is recomputed on every request; that is the problem.

prompt: Why does the export write `manifest.json` last?
hint: What does its presence tell the reader?

choices.text: JSON files have to be written after CSV files on Linux
choices.why: There is no such rule; the order is an agreement between writer and reader.

choices.text: So its checksum includes its own bytes
choices.why: The checksum is of `rides.csv`, not of the manifest.

choices.text: Because the manifest is the smallest file and the quickest to write
choices.why: Size is irrelevant; order is the signal.

choices.text: Its presence says the data before it is complete
choices.why: Right: a reader touches nothing until it exists.

prompt: How many rows did the plain `load.py` take from the interrupted export?
hint: The line after `python load.py`.

prompt: Why did the plain load of the half-written file print no error?
hint: Look at the last row it printed.

choices.text: Python catches CSV errors and hides them by default
choices.why: There was no error to hide; the reader accepted the line.

choices.text: `csv.DictReader` filled the short row with `None`
choices.why: Right: a half row became a plausible-looking record.

choices.text: The export wrote a complete last row before it stopped
choices.why: The last row has station `ST`: it was cut in the middle.

choices.text: The manifest said 718 rows, and the load matched it
choices.why: There was no manifest; that is why the careful load refused.

prompt: A reader polls a bucket and loads any file that has not grown for ten minutes, on the grounds that its writer must have finished. What is wrong with that rule?
hint: What else stops a file from growing?

choices.text: Ten minutes is too short; an hour would make it safe
choices.why: No wait tells a finished writer from a dead one.

choices.text: Buckets do not report when a file last changed
choices.why: They do; the trouble is what the time means.

choices.text: A dead writer’s file stops growing too
choices.why: Right: only a marker written last says the writer finished.

choices.text: Polling a bucket costs more than reading a manifest
choices.why: Cost is beside the point; the rule loads half files.

prompt: Why is every field `parse_log.py` prints a string, even the status code?
hint: What does a regular expression return?

choices.text: The log stores numbers as text to save space
choices.why: Text is not smaller; a regular expression simply finds text.

choices.text: A regular expression finds text, and turning it into numbers is a later step
choices.why: Right: converting the types is a separate, later step.

choices.text: `groupdict` converts numbers back to strings for printing
choices.why: It never had numbers to convert.

choices.text: Status codes like `404` are not really numbers in HTTP
choices.why: They are numbers; the parser just has not converted them.

prompt: Why does `parse_log.py` list the line numbers it could not parse instead of skipping them?
hint: Think of the day the log format changes.

choices.text: To delete them from the log afterwards
choices.why: The source is not edited; the reader reports.

choices.text: Because Python’s `re` module requires it
choices.why: It requires nothing of the kind; this is a choice.

choices.text: So that a broken format is noticed soon
choices.why: Right: a skipping parser would drop every line just as quietly.

choices.text: To count the broken lines as failed requests
choices.why: A cut-off line is not a failed request; its status is unknown.

prompt: The log has a `500` and then a `200` for `/v1/rides/R000301/end`, two seconds apart. What happened to the customer?
hint: Read the two lines together.

choices.text: Two rides were ended, one with an error
choices.why: Both lines name the same ride, `R000301`.

choices.text: One ride, which ended when the app retried
choices.why: Right: one ride, ended two seconds late.

choices.text: The ride is still open, because a `500` cancels the request
choices.why: The `200` after it says the second attempt worked.

choices.text: Two different customers tried to end the same ride
choices.why: Both requests came from one address and one app.

prompt: Why does a web server’s access log count as personal data under the LGPD, though it holds no names?
hint: Look at the first field of every line.

choices.text: It records every customer’s password in each request
choices.why: The combined format holds no passwords.

choices.text: The LGPD covers every file a company stores
choices.why: It covers information that relates to a person, not files as such.

choices.text: Its first field is an address that identifies people
choices.why: Right: information that identifies a person is personal data, named or not.

choices.text: The user agent names the customer’s phone owner
choices.why: It names the app and the system, not the person.

prompt: Writing each line of a log as a JSON object, so the fields arrive already named, is called ___ logging.
hint: The opposite of a sentence for a person.

prompt: What do application events record that the app’s database does not?
hint: A customer looked at a station and closed the app.

choices.text: The current state of every ride and bicycle
choices.why: That is what the database keeps.

choices.text: The passwords customers sign in with
choices.why: Events are about actions in the app, not credentials.

choices.text: Actions that change no row
choices.why: Right: opening the map, looking, giving up.

choices.text: The charges the payments provider has made
choices.why: Those are at the provider, read through its API.

prompt: Why does at-least-once delivery write some events twice?
hint: What can the phone not tell apart?

choices.text: The collector copies each event to two servers
choices.why: Copies for safety are not duplicates in the data.

choices.text: To the phone, a lost reply looks like a lost event
choices.why: Right: so the phone resends, and the collector already had it.

choices.text: The app sends each event twice on purpose, as a check
choices.why: It sends once and resends only when it hears nothing back.

choices.text: Two versions of the app are installed on each phone
choices.why: One app per phone; the duplicate comes from the network.

prompt: Two `ride_started` events from one customer arrive a second apart, with the same `event_id`. What are they?
hint: The phone gave the id when it created the event.

choices.text: Two rides, started a second apart
choices.why: Two rides would carry two ids.

choices.text: A customer who tapped the button twice
choices.why: Each tap creates an event with its own id.

choices.text: A bug in the collector, to be reported to its vendor
choices.why: It is the normal price of at-least-once delivery.

choices.text: One event that the phone sent twice, having heard no answer the first time
choices.why: Right: one id is one event, and the copy is removed.

prompt: Without a tracking plan, app 3.3 sends `rideStarted` and app 3.4 sends `ride_started`. A dashboard counts `ride_started`. What does it show over the month after 3.4 ships?
hint: Customers do not all update on the same day.

choices.text: A count that is right from the day 3.4 is released
choices.why: Phones still on 3.3 send the other name.

choices.text: Rides rising as phones update
choices.why: Right: the growth is in the app version, not in the rides.

choices.text: Every ride counted twice, once under each name
choices.why: Each phone sends one name, and only one is counted.

choices.text: An error, because the dashboard refuses unknown event names
choices.why: Unknown names are ignored, not refused; that is the trouble.

prompt: Match each field of an event to what it is for.
hint: One of them is the only defence against duplicates.

pairs.right: telling a resend from a new event
the phone’s clock, which the customer controls
when it arrived, by a clock you trust
which build of the app sent it

prompt: How many readings arrived twice in the hour `docks.py` made?
hint: The third line of output.

prompt: 185 readings arrived where 180 were due. Why is that not a sign that the hour is complete?
hint: Remove the ones that came twice.

choices.text: The sensors send extra readings when a bicycle is docked
choices.why: They send one a minute; the extra ones are resends.

choices.text: Eleven came twice, which hides six readings that never came at all
choices.why: Right: 185 minus 11 is 174, six short of 180.

choices.text: The server counts each reading once per sensor and once per station
choices.why: There is one count; it includes resends.

choices.text: Five readings came from a fourth dock that was not in the list
choices.why: There are three docks; the surplus is duplicates.

prompt: What does a sequence number on each reading make possible?
hint: It goes up by one every reading.

choices.text: Correcting the sensor’s clock
choices.why: Clocks are corrected with NTP; the number says nothing about time.

choices.text: Counting the gaps and the duplicates
choices.why: Right: a missing number is a gap, a number seen twice a duplicate.

choices.text: Sending readings without a network
choices.why: It is a label on the reading, not a way to send it.

choices.text: Encrypting the readings on the way
choices.why: Numbering is not encryption.

prompt: A program keeps, for each dock, whichever reading reached the server most recently, and calls it the dock’s current state. What goes wrong?
hint: Six readings arrived after a later one.

choices.text: Nothing, because readings arrive in the order they were taken
choices.why: Six of them did not, in one hour of three docks.

choices.text: It counts each duplicate as a second bicycle
choices.why: Keeping one reading per dock counts no bicycles twice.

choices.text: It crashes when two readings arrive in the same second
choices.why: A tie in arrival time is not an error.

choices.text: An old reading that was delayed replaces a newer one
choices.why: Right: order by sequence number, not by arrival.

prompt: 57 readings from `ST02-D02` are stamped later than the moment they reached the server. What does that say?
hint: No reading arrives before it is taken.

choices.text: The network delivered them faster than light allows
choices.why: The network was ordinary; the stamp is wrong.

choices.text: That sensor’s clock runs ahead of the real time
choices.why: Right: by 47 seconds, which moves every empty spell it reports.

choices.text: The server’s clock is in UTC and the sensor’s is in São Paulo time
choices.why: That would be three hours, not 47 seconds, and on every dock.

choices.text: Those readings are duplicates and should be removed
choices.why: Duplicates share a sequence number; these do not.

prompt: What turns a written list of a source owner’s answers into a data contract?
hint: Look at the `key` and `expected` lines.

choices.text: A signature from the company’s legal team
choices.why: It is not a legal document.

choices.text: Writing it in a standard format such as JSON
choices.why: There is no single standard format; YAML or a wiki page also serve.

choices.text: Both sides agree to it, and a program checks it
choices.why: Right: the checks are what make the promise hold.

choices.text: The data team writes it without the owner, so it stays neutral
choices.why: It is the producer’s promise; without the owner it promises nothing.

prompt: The sensor vendor refuses to number its readings. What belongs in the dock readings’ contract?
hint: A contract also records what was not promised.

choices.text: The vendor’s refusal, written down as a known gap
choices.why: Right: next year’s engineer finds it written down.

choices.text: A sequence number the data team adds on arrival
choices.why: Numbering on arrival counts what arrived, so it shows no gaps.

choices.text: Nothing about numbering, since the vendor would not agree to it
choices.why: Leaving it out is how the next person rediscovers the problem.

choices.text: A clause that ends the vendor’s contract if a reading goes missing
choices.why: A data contract records behaviour; it is not a commercial agreement.

prompt: Put the careful loader’s steps in order.
hint: Nothing is parsed until it is known to be whole.
items: compare their SHA-256 with the manifest
trap: The checksum can only be compared once the bytes are read, and parsing comes after both checks.

prompt: Match each quiet failure to what prevents it.
hint: One remedy per section of the lesson.

pairs.left: a cancelled ride stays in the copy
a resent event is counted twice

pairs.right: waiting and asking for it again

prompt: Marta asks how many rides were cancelled in September. The data team has only the incremental copy of the rides table. What does the copy say?
hint: The app deletes cancelled rides.

choices.text: The right number, since each cancellation updates `updated_at`
choices.why: A cancellation here is a delete, and a deleted row updates nothing.

choices.text: Zero, and the cancelled rides look open
choices.why: Right: the copy cannot answer, and does not know it cannot.

choices.text: An error, because the cancelled rows are missing
choices.why: Missing rows raise nothing; that is the trouble.

choices.text: Twice the real number, once for the ride and once for the delete
choices.why: The copy never receives the delete, so it cannot count it.

prompt: A partner sends payment records with at-least-once delivery and no identifier on each record. Two identical records arrive. What can nobody tell?
hint: Compare with `event_id`.

choices.text: Whether either record is a payment at all
choices.why: The records say what they are; the question is how many.

choices.text: Which time zone the records were written in
choices.why: Time zone is a separate question for the owner.

choices.text: Whether the partner’s API has a rate limit
choices.why: Rate limits do not create identical records.

choices.text: Whether it is one payment resent or two payments
choices.why: Right: without an id they look the same, so ask for one first.
